paragraphs.text: Everything on this page hangs on one picture: the wall calendar of the Dobart family. Four people, one week, and a lot of handwriting. Hannes is away, Mara has shifts, Florian and Lena have lessons and rehearsals. Before you write a single German sentence, read that calendar the way you would read your own — who is where, and when.

German answers two different questions about time, and the preposition tells you which one you are answering. {{de:Wann?}} asks for a single point: {{de:am Montag}}, {{de:um drei Uhr}}, {{de:um Viertel nach vier}}. {{de:Wie lange?}} asks for a stretch of time, and that is what {{de:von}} … {{de:bis}} is built for: {{de:von Sonntag bis Dienstag}}, {{de:von 9 bis 17 Uhr}}. Days take {{de:am}}, clock times take {{de:um}}. Get those two straight now and every timetable you ever read will be readable.
Hannes ist von Sonntag bis Dienstag in Hamburg. Mara arbeitet am Freitag von 9 bis 17 Uhr. Lena hat am Montag um fünf Uhr Geigenunterricht.

One habit worth copying from the last lesson: 17:00 on the calendar becomes {{de:um fünf Uhr}} when the family talks about it and stays {{de:siebzehn Uhr}} on a train schedule. The family's own speech uses the small numbers, so {{de:fünfzehn Uhr fünfzehn}} in an email and {{de:viertel nach drei}} at the kitchen table are both correct — they are simply two different rooms.

paragraphs.text: The pronunciation drill on this page asks you to sort ten words into two piles: where you hear a real r, and where you do not. Say {{de:Hören}}, {{de:Vater}}, {{de:Uhr}} and {{de:Computer}} out loud. At the end of a word, and inside the syllable ending -er, German lets the r soften towards the vowel you already know from the end of {{de:Kamera}} — the tongue never rolls up there.
hören · Vater · Tochter · treffen · Schwester · krank · Uhr · Büro · Trompete · Computer

A rolled r in {{de:Vater}} will still be understood, but it sounds like you are reading the word rather than saying it. Keep the strong r at the start of a word — {{de:Regen}}, {{de:Raum}}, {{de:rufen}} — and let the end of the word go soft. The same soft sound is what you hear in {{de:Siebzehn Uhr}} and in the last syllable of {{de:Mutter}}.

blocks.prompt: Fill the gap with the right time expression from the calendar.

paragraphs.text: Go back to the Dobart calendar before you answer. If the gap names a day or an hour, the sentence is asking {{de:Wann?}}; if it names a stretch, it is asking {{de:Wie lange?}} and you need {{de:von … bis}}.

blocks.passage: Die Eltern sind Hannes und Mara. Die Kinder sind Florian und Lena.
blocks.prompt: Who are the children in this family?
blocks.explanationEnglish: Die Eltern are the parents, Hannes and Mara. Florian and Lena are die Kinder — the son and the daughter.

concept.title: die Eltern und die Kinder
concept.rule: Die Eltern means the parents together — father and mother as one pair. Die Kinder are the children of that pair. A single child is das Kind; the plural is die Kinder.
concept.exampleGerman: Die Eltern arbeiten, die Kinder gehen in die Schule.
concept.exampleEnglish: The parents work, the children go to school.
